q: Will banks see a second purchase this year as too aggressive, will the tax office come asking, and how can he improve his chances?
situation: C spent months watching Sean's videos, viewing projects, listing pros and cons and preparing his loan documents before signing the SPA for his first property two weeks ago; his loan offer came in three days. He now wants to buy a second property this year.
reference:
Sean's words: "We can declare rent that we collect as income."
His answer: Banks and the tax office don't mind how many properties you buy; they care whether you can repay and where your money comes from. If the first property is rented out, its rent can count as income for the next loan after about six months of records, so a rented subsale can lead to a second purchase quickly. If it's your home, the instalment simply reduces what you can borrow.
Why:
- Rent can add to your borrowing power: With a tenancy agreement and at least six months of rent paid into your account, some banks count 100% of the rent as income and others 80%. A RM2,000 instalment with RM2,200 rent leaves you better off for the next loan, not worse.
- Tax is on profit, not rent: Declared rent is taxable, but loan interest and other costs can be deducted, and in the first years most of the instalment is interest. The authorities mainly want to see where your money came from, such as an inheritance or gift.
- Subsales move faster than new launches: A subsale completes in about four to six months and can be let straight away, so its rent starts counting sooner. A new launch takes four to five years to complete, which is a long wait before the next step.
- The rules can tighten: Two 90% loans per person, low upfront payments and current RPGT rates are policies, not permanent features. Earlier rules differed and future ones could be stricter, which is a reason to act while the terms are favourable.
What he told them to do:
- Rent out the first property if you can live elsewhere cheaply, such as with family.
- Keep the tenancy agreement and make sure rent is paid into your bank account every month.
- Declare the rental income and keep records of interest and costs to deduct.
- Budget about 18% of the price in cash for a subsale, plus about RM50,000 to RM80,000 to furnish it.
- Keep six to eight months of expenses and your insurance in place before taking on a second loan.
When it does not apply: Sean thinks most people only need two or three properties in a lifetime, not dozens. If the first purchase is your home, expect to wait for your income to grow before the second.

q: Is it possible to borrow on the higher valuation so the purchase is effectively 100% financed, and how does the process work?
situation: M is a first-time buyer looking at a subsale apartment in Maluri listed at RM260,000, with a market valuation of about RM280,000. M doesn't want to use up savings on the 10% down payment and other costs, and hopes to negotiate the price down to RM245,000 while borrowing RM280,000, using the difference for the down payment, fees and renovation.
reference:
Sean's words: "Maybe you cannot afford the property."
His answer: Not simply: banks lend up to 90% of the price written in the SPA, not the valuation, and every fee and tax follows that SPA figure too. If the down payment and costs would wipe out your savings, either save a little longer, look at EPF withdrawals or genuine full-financing schemes, or accept that the property may be beyond your budget for now.
Why:
- The SPA price sets the loan: Stamp duty, legal fees and any RPGT are all calculated on the SPA price. Writing a higher price raises the owner's and buyer's costs, so owners often refuse, and any such arrangement depends on the bank's own valuation, the owner's written consent through the lawyers, and your income qualifying for the larger loan.
- Valuations come from the bank: An agent's figure isn't enough: the bank asks its panel valuers, who may quote different amounts. Even a high valuation only helps if you qualify for the bigger loan.
- A subsale needs about 18% in cash: Beyond the 10% down payment come legal fees, stamp duty and other charges, paid in stages over a six- to nine-month process. It's easy to lose track, so budget for the whole amount from the start.
- Owning costs more than the instalment: Maintenance, repairs and building levies add up. If the instalment is well above what you'd pay in rent, and you're single with an uncertain future, renting and investing first may be the better path.
What he told them to do:
- Budget about 18% of the price in cash before committing to a subsale.
- Check how much you could withdraw from EPF towards a purchase under the current rules.
- Ask banks whether you qualify for any genuine full-financing scheme for first homes.
- If buying would leave no emergency fund, set a savings target, such as another RM10,000 in six to eight months, before buying.
- Have any unusual price arrangement checked by your own lawyer before signing anything.
When it does not apply: If the price is a rare bargain and you can live without savings for a year or two, buying now can still be your choice; Sean asks whether your health, family and sleep can handle that. Sean also stresses he is not an agent and sells no property.

q: Should she sell the house and put the money into EPF, or keep it?
situation: YC's mother is in her 60s. She owns a single-storey leasehold house in Ampang worth about RM360,000, let for RM1,200 a month, with about 64 years left on the lease; she has heard banks are reluctant to lend once fewer than 60 years remain. She also owns a fully paid apartment and a shop lot, both rented out, and herself rents a double-storey house in OUG for convenience.
reference:
Sean's words: "I will never sell any property unless it's losing money."
His answer: Keep it. The house is paid off and its rent sustains itself, and the leasehold issue will matter more to her heirs than to her. If she wants more cash for peace of mind, refinance the apartment or shop lot only as far as their rent can repay, rather than selling an asset that pays its way.
Why:
- A self-sustaining property has no reason to go: With no loan and steady rent, the house costs her nothing to hold. Sean would only sell a property that loses money, or if she truly needs the cash.
- Leases can be extended: Sean says Selangor lets owners apply to renew a lease to 99 years for a fee, with conditions on a later sale, and points to a Penang building where a renewal lifted values sharply. Whether the house falls under Selangor or Kuala Lumpur decides which rules apply.
- Refinancing beats selling for cash: Borrowing against the shop lot or apartment, only up to what the rent repays, releases cash at housing loan rates while she keeps the assets. Sean's example: a RM2 million shop lot renting at RM10,000 a month could free about RM1 million at her age.
- Renting where you live is good value: Double-storey terraces in OUG cost about RM1.4 million to RM1.6 million, but renting one is far cheaper, and her rental income covers it.
What he told them to do:
- Check the title to see whether the house is under Selangor or Kuala Lumpur, and ask the land office about extending the lease.
- Decide what the cash is for: safety, travel, charity or leaving more to the family.
- If she needs cash, compare refinancing the apartment or shop lot with selling the house.
- Keep enough insurance, such as MRTA or MLTA, on any new loan so it never passes to the family as debt.
- Talk as a family about how the properties will be passed on.
When it does not apply: If she simply feels safer with money in EPF, selling isn't wrong; it just gives up a property that pays for itself. Lease renewal rules and fees vary by state and change, so confirm them with the land office.

q: Should he buy an investment property now despite his budget, or keep saving for his dream landed home?
situation: Mr N, 33, takes home about RM10,000 a month, has two young children and lives with his parents. After insurance, a car loan, a RM2,700 housing loan, food, his mother's allowance and other costs he has about RM2,500 left each month, plus about RM75,000 in crypto. He is weighing a studio or two-room condo of up to RM700,000 as an investment in 2024 against saving for 12 years to buy a corner terrace house in Kwasa Land or Elmina in his late 40s.
reference:
Sean's words: "I think the proposition here is to own the apartment first."
His answer: Buy an investment unit first, but a smaller one than RM700,000: an instalment of about RM2,000 to RM2,500, on a unit where current rents already cover it. Let it build equity for 10 to 12 years, then sell it for the down payment on the terrace house, instead of chasing prices with savings alone.
Why:
- Savings rarely catch property prices: Elmina Green homes launched at about RM600,000 to RM700,000, and later phases cost about RM1.2 million. A friend of Sean's saved for years for a Shah Alam terrace as its price kept moving out of reach.
- A RM4,000 instalment is too much stress: His income could get a loan of about RM1 million, but a RM4,000 instalment with two children leaves no room if the unit sits empty or his job changes. About RM2,000 to RM2,500 a month is his sweet spot, roughly a RM500,000 to RM600,000 unit.
- Build in a safety factor: Choose a unit where rents nearby already cover the instalment, so it still works if rents fall 10% by completion. And budget about RM50,000 for furnishing so it can be let as soon as the keys arrive.
- Crypto isn't a plan: Money in crypto should be money he can afford to lose overnight, not the foundation for a home.
What he told them to do:
- Set your instalment limit at about RM2,000 to RM2,500 a month and search for units at that price.
- Check current rents for each shortlisted unit, and make sure a 10% drop still covers the instalment.
- Save bonuses towards a furnishing budget of about RM50,000 for handover.
- With little time for research, consider paying for professional deal sourcing and data.
- Plan to sell the unit in 10 to 12 years to fund the down payment on your terrace house.
When it does not apply: This depends on his job staying secure; if it doesn't, a smaller unit or waiting is safer. Sean points to a bulk purchase club he is a VIP member of and buys from, which he says he doesn't run.

q: Should they rent out or sell the Bangi house, is RM3,200 a month a burden, and what are Cyberjaya's prospects if they sell in 20 years?
situation: E, 40, and her husband are civil servants who have lived in a Bangi terrace house since 2014, now valued at about RM430,000 to RM530,000. Their son's playschool is in Cyberjaya and E works in Putrajaya, a journey of about 90 minutes. They are looking at a Cyberjaya condo due in 2025, with a loan of about RM575,000 over 29 years and about RM3,200 a month including maintenance, though E retires in 19 years.
reference:
Sean's words: "We rent things that depreciates in value."
His answer: First check the numbers they left out: their joint income and how much is still owed on the Bangi house. Cyberjaya high-rises have generally lost value, so before committing RM3,200 a month for 29 years, compare about 20 projects nearby, consider Putrajaya, or simply rent in Cyberjaya, which is cheap for the space you get.
Why:
- Selling may free less than you think: In the first years of a loan most of each instalment goes to interest, so a house bought around RM400,000 may still owe about RM380,000 after ten years. After any RPGT on the gain, the cash arrives six to eight months after the sale.
- Cyberjaya high-rises have struggled: The town has jobs and amenities, but rental demand hasn't followed, and many condos end up at auction. A friend of Sean's bought at RM450,000 ten years ago; similar units now go for about RM280,000.
- Rent what loses value: Where high-rise prices are falling, rents are low too, so a bigger unit or even a landed home can be rented for less than the RM3,200 instalment. Distances in Cyberjaya are also quick to drive, so living right beside the school isn't essential.
- Sales galleries are built to close: Sean once designed sales galleries and says most buyers who walk in end up booking. Comparing other projects, and Putrajaya, which has performed better, protects against an emotional purchase.
What he told them to do:
- Work out your joint income and check the instalment is no more than about a third of it.
- Find out how much you still owe on the Bangi house and what it would sell for after costs.
- Visit about 20 projects around Cyberjaya and Putrajaya, including subsales, before booking.
- Price what RM2,500 to RM2,600 a month would rent in Cyberjaya, and compare it with buying.
- If you keep the Bangi house to rent out, don't expect a landed home's rent to cover a loan.
When it does not apply: If one specific school is non-negotiable, living nearby matters more. Sean notes Cyberjaya's landed homes have done well; his concern is its high-rise market.

q: How many properties should he aim for, where and how should he source them, and how should he rent and manage them?
situation: D is 30, married with a baby due in 2024, and is returning from working overseas to live in Sabah, where his home is sorted. He has about RM1 million to invest in property, up to RM1.5 million if needed, a share portfolio yielding about 5%, no debts and will earn about RM10,000 a month. He finds Sabah prices high against local incomes and is open to buying in West Malaysia, landed or high-rise, aiming for rent that covers 80% of the repayment.
reference:
Sean's words: "The goal is to buy money making properties."
His answer: Don't aim for a number of properties: three good ones beat six weak ones. Before buying anything, visit about 20 properties across types, areas and both sides of Malaysia, learn the four ways to buy, and never pay above the median price. Keep the money in shares meanwhile; property prices won't run away in a year.
Why:
- Counting properties leads to bad buys: Chasing a target makes it tempting to add small, weak units just to raise the count. Adding a property feels good, like a new pair of shoes, but the aim is income and wealth.
- Where you buy changes the price you pay: Buying from a developer usually means the full retail price; a subsale gives certainty and room to negotiate; auctions often end near market price and can hide caveats and unpaid maintenance; bulk purchases can unlock deals individuals never see.
- Local markets behave differently: Sabah and Sarawak don't see Kuala Lumpur's flood of launches, and some landed homes in Kota Kinabalu and Kuching have grown well, so oversupply isn't a nationwide fact. Living in Sabah gives him local knowledge worth using.
- His income sets the pace: Cash isn't his limit; a RM10,000 salary is, perhaps RM3,000 to RM4,000 a month for instalments. Buying one property at a time and declaring its rent as income keeps his debt service ratio healthy for the next.
What he told them to do:
- Visit about 20 properties of different types and areas, in Sabah and West Malaysia, before buying.
- Compare developer, subsale, auction and bulk purchase prices for the same kind of unit.
- Check the median price in each area and don't buy above it.
- Buy one at a time, let the first unit's rent show in your income records, then buy the next.
- Consider your wife's name and loan eligibility for a later purchase.
When it does not apply: Sean wouldn't name specific projects: the same unit can cost different buyers different prices depending on their access to deals. His bulk purchase suggestion comes from a group he is a customer of.

q: Was the price too high, is there room for growth, should he use the overdraft to buy more, and how does anyone keep buying property after property?
situation: Mr T runs the family eatery in his hometown and is nearly 50. He and his wife own a bungalow bought for RM717,000 in 2011, with about RM300,000 left on a flexi loan with an overdraft facility, plus an inherited shop lot and old house. After spending heavily on renovation and their three children's international education, they have about RM400,000 to RM500,000 saved. His wife has just bought a 460 sq ft unit in Bandar Sunway at about RM1,250 per sq ft, let to students at about RM2,700 a month; the previous owner paid RM517,000 in 2017.
reference:
Sean's words: "I do not look at what was the purchase price of the previous buyer."
His answer: Judge the price against today's market and the rent, not against what the first owner paid. With a normal 90% loan the rent would roughly cover the instalment, so it isn't a bad buy, and in a fully built-up area growth will come from rising rents rather than new projects. To keep buying, let rent count as income for the next loan.
Why:
- Compare with today, not 2017: Few people would have bought back then anyway. Check the price per square foot of similar units nearby and the yield: a 90% loan of about RM513,000 over 35 years at 4% costs about RM2,600 a month, against a tenancy of about RM2,700.
- Mature areas grow through rent: With trains, universities and malls already in place, new infrastructure won't add much. But as student demand pushes rents up, investors will pay more for a unit whose rent covers their instalment, and that becomes the exit.
- Rent can help you borrow again: Banks count rent shown by a tenancy agreement, six months of bank statements and the SPA, usually at 80% and at some banks 100%. On a RM5,000 salary, a RM1,500 instalment with RM1,700 rent leaves more borrowing power than before the purchase.
- An overdraft is like refinancing: Drawing on the flexi loan's overdraft costs much the same as refinancing the bungalow. With the children moving out, downsizing from a 6,300 sq ft bungalow would free more cash than either.
What he told them to do:
- Check recent prices per square foot and rents for similar units around Bandar Sunway to judge what you paid.
- Buy units where the rent covers the instalment, so each one adds to your borrowing power for the next.
- Keep tenancy agreements and six months of rent records ready for your next loan application.
- Look for below-market prices at auctions or through bulk purchases; a subsale is usually at market price.
- Spend on renovation only what keeps a home practical, since heavy renovation adds little at resale.
When it does not apply: Sean doesn't treat transit-oriented development as essential: developers already price it in, and units without a train link can still yield well. He couldn't comment on a new project's value before its prices were known.

q: Is it better to buy with a loan or in cash, and can M take housing loans for two properties at once on this salary?
situation: M is 23 and earns RM3,500 a month. M's father has given M RM800,000 in cash, RM500,000 in shares, RM130,000 in a unit trust and two houses worth about RM1.2 million; the family owns five other properties, mostly bought in cash. M wants to buy an apartment in Cheras for about RM200,000 to RM300,000 as an investment, with an instalment of about RM1,300, but M's parents would rather pay cash to save interest.
reference:
Sean's words: "Your active income will be the limiting factor."
His answer: Use loans for the first two purchases, while the 90% margin is available, and leave the cash in fixed deposits; the tenant's rent pays the interest. Buy one at a time: after about six months of rent records the bank counts the rent as income for the next loan. Cash comes in later, for a third property at 70% and for furnishing.
Why:
- Cheap loans favour leverage: M's parents bought when interest rates were around 10% to 12%, so paying cash made sense. With rates far lower, it's better to use the bank's money and keep the cash working.
- Rent becomes income: If the rent is a little above the instalment, the surplus adds to M's income for the next loan once there is a tenancy agreement and six months of payments. Two loans at once won't pass on RM3,500 a month.
- Cash has its turn later: The third housing loan is capped at 70%, so a RM500,000 unit needs about RM150,000 down; furnishing a RM300,000 subsale to let may cost RM30,000 to RM40,000. The gifted houses can also be refinanced, if M's income supports it.
- Income is the real limit: Every loan and refinance depends on M's own income, so building skills and a career matters as much as the assets. Having more to lose also means more care: learn, take advice and run due diligence.
What he told them to do:
- Buy the first unit with a loan, but only if the rent covers the instalment.
- Keep the cash in fixed deposits and leave the shares as they are while you learn.
- Set a furnishing budget for each unit so it rents well from day one.
- Wait about six months after letting the first unit before applying for the second loan.
- Learn how rental and dividend income are declared and taxed, so they count towards future loans.
When it does not apply: Sean respects the parents' cash approach, which suited the high rates of their time. The plan depends on the rent covering each instalment; if it doesn't, paying more upfront is the safer route.

q: Is the student unit a good investment, and is buying a second property for own use in the same year too fast?
situation: A is 23, earns about RM20,000 a month freelancing and has RM200,000 saved. A plans to buy a RM590,000 subsale unit within walking distance of a university, already partitioned and let to students, expecting about RM3,500 a month in rent against a RM2,450 instalment plus about RM1,000 for maintenance, Wi-Fi and utilities. A also wants a RM500,000 to RM800,000 home in Ara Damansara or Kota Damansara within the same year.
reference:
Sean's words: "I think you are on the right track, bro."
His answer: Yes: about RM42,000 a year in rent on RM590,000 is a 7.1% yield, well above fixed deposits and the loan rate. But budget about 18% of the price upfront, understand the partition and exit risks, and use the second 90% loan on another investment rather than a home while young and mobile.
Why:
- The yield is unusually high: With loan rates around 3.85% to 4%, a yield of about 4% covers the interest and 5% is already good. Over 7% is usually only found near universities, in busy expatriate areas or in holiday spots, each with their own risks.
- Partitions bring legal and insurance risk: Kuala Lumpur City Hall has moved to ban partitioned living rooms, and partitions built without approval can void the fire insurance. Rent that depends on them may not last.
- Student units sell only to investors: Families rarely want to live among student tenants, so the buyer later is another investor who prices by rent. If rents rise, the value rises with them, but if a nearby campus moves, demand can go too.
- A home can wait: At 23 and working freelance, renting in a cheaper suburb such as Cyberjaya keeps costs low and options open. With this income, a second investment can be financed without waiting for the first unit's rent records.
What he told them to do:
- Budget about 18% of the price for down payment, stamp duty and fees, about RM106,000 here, before any renovation.
- Check whether the existing partitions were approved, and what rent the unit would earn without them.
- Check that the university nearby is a main campus that is unlikely to move, not a branch run from shop lots.
- Declare your full income for tax: it costs a little more but helps the bank approve larger loans.
- Keep six months of expenses and insurance in place, and learn other assets with small regular amounts.
When it does not apply: If you want to live in a property later, the 85% rule applies instead: rent should cover at least 85% of the instalment so you can rent it out when you move. Sean assumed the income is steady; freelance income that varies changes the picture.

q: Should he buy the property outright with his father's cash, or take a housing loan?
situation: Low works in Singapore. His father has offered to pay cash, just under RM1 million, for a property, or alternatively to help with the down payment while Low pays the instalments himself. Low plans to rent it out for a few years and live in it when he moves back to Malaysia.
reference:
Sean's words: "I will go for loan because it gives me more flexibility."
His answer: Take a loan. Either park the cash in a full flexi loan to cut the interest while keeping it withdrawable, use it to buy two or three high-yield subsale investments, or keep it invested elsewhere while the rent pays the loan. Paying fully in cash ties everything up in one illiquid asset.
Why:
- Property is hard to turn back into cash: A purchase takes six to eight months to complete, selling quickly means selling below market, you can't refinance without built-up equity, and unlike shares you can't sell part of it in an emergency.
- A flexi loan saves interest and stays liquid: Interest is calculated daily on what you owe, and in the early years about 88% to 90% of each instalment is interest. Parking the cash in a full flexi account cuts that sharply, and you can still withdraw it.
- Capital opens the subsale market: Few young buyers can pay about 18% upfront, about RM144,000 on an RM800,000 subsale plus RM50,000 to RM80,000 for renovation. With it, you can see the unit, its rent and neighbours' prices first, and buy only at 5.5% to 6% yield or better.
- Interest is less scary than it looks: A RM500,000 loan over 35 years costs about RM429,000 in interest, but property has risen about 4.3% to 4.5% a year over the past decade, and inflation shrinks the real value of that interest over time.
What he told them to do:
- Buy with a housing loan and place the cash in a full flexi account to reduce interest.
- Or, use the capital for one subsale at a time: buy, furnish, rent out, then use six months of rent records for the next loan.
- Set a minimum yield, such as 5.5% to 6% of the price, before buying any investment unit.
- Buy for a clear purpose, investment or own stay, not a 'just in case' home for when you return.
- Ask your father what he intends the money for, and show him a plan for how you would use it.
When it does not apply: If your father's wish is simply to give you a fully paid home, and the sum is a small part of his wealth, buying in cash is not wrong. Sean also warns against putting family money into friends' business ventures you don't understand.

q: Should K buy gold instead, take the resale unit, or look at high-density projects around Sunway Velocity?
situation: K works in New Zealand, where mortgage rates are 7% to 8%, and takes home about RM12,000 a month. A condo in Taman Desa is rented out and covers its repayment, and K plans to settle its remaining RM69,000 loan within months. K is considering a resale unit of about RM467,000 near an MRT station in Kuala Lumpur, with a 10% rebate, but nearby rents suggest a RM500 to RM600 monthly top-up. Family members say gold is the better buy right now.
reference:
Sean's words: "Why must you settle for a project that cannot make money?"
His answer: Don't commit to a unit you already know will cost you RM500 to RM600 a month; keep looking until you find one where the rent covers the instalment. As for gold, check whether the people recommending it have the results you want, and invest in what you understand.
Why:
- Judge the advice by the adviser: Tips from relatives are often second-hand, from a short video or a sales commission. Sean puts his money in property because he knows it well, and sees the asset you understand best as the safest one.
- There are always other projects: Buyers often fix on one development, then blame the developer or the market when it doesn't pay. Sean says view 20 projects of different types, ages and areas and move on from any that can't make money.
- Developers sell at the recommended retail price: Investors try to buy below it: through subsale, where the owner's urgency gives room to negotiate; auctions, which can carry caveats, title problems or unpaid maintenance; or bulk purchase deals.
- Settling a covered loan may waste cash: The Taman Desa rent already covers its instalment, so paying off the last RM69,000 may not be the best use of the money; it could fund another unit where the rent covers the loan. Sean couldn't judge this fully without knowing K's age.
What he told them to do:
- Ask whoever recommends gold or any other investment whether they have invested in it themselves and got the results you want.
- Drop any unit whose rent won't cover the instalment, however close it is to a station.
- View around 20 projects of different types and locations before choosing.
- Compare subsale, auction and bulk purchase prices against the developer's price.
- Before settling a loan the rent already covers, compare that with using the cash as a down payment elsewhere.
When it does not apply: Sean sees no legal problem with a unit resold after the first buyer's SPA was cancelled. Auctions are harder to manage from overseas, so he wouldn't suggest them for K.

q: How should a young doctor start investing, and can REITs replace buying property?
situation: A, 26, is waiting for his housemanship placement in a government hospital, where take-home pay starts at about RM4,000 to RM4,500. He has no savings yet, lives with his parents, works part-time and may be posted to any state. He wants to know how doctors can grow a portfolio given their long studies, whether to buy an investment unit he might live in later, and whether REITs are an alternative to property.
reference:
Sean's words: "It's not a real estate alternative, it's a stock alternative."
His answer: Don't rush to buy: property needs active income and credit, and his will grow. Use the next few years to save, avoid upgrading his lifestyle with each pay rise, learn by investing small sums, and buy investment property first once he earns about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month. REITs are fine, but they behave like shares, not property.
Why:
- Income and credit drive property investing: Investors with seven or eight properties usually earn RM15,000 to RM20,000 a month. For Sean, property is a way to diversify wealth as income rises, not a quick money maker, so starting at 36 or even 46 is fine.
- Lifestyle creep is the real danger: As pay rises, people upgrade cars, homes and habits and save nothing more. Putting the extra into something that pays cash flow, starting with dividend shares or fixed deposits, builds the habit.
- Investment and own-stay homes differ: High-yield units sit near jobs, transport and malls, while good family homes are quiet and low density, where tenants rarely rent. Buying one to rent now and live in later usually does neither well, and his postings could take him anywhere.
- REITs lack property's leverage: Malaysian REITs yield about 4.8% to 5% and trade like shares. RM50,000 put into a RM400,000 subsale with a RM360,000 loan can bring about RM19,200 a year in rent that covers the instalment, while the asset itself can grow, though it takes far more work.
What he told them to do:
- Build your emergency fund first, and keep your insurance in place.
- Learn to invest with small amounts, such as dividend-paying blue chips, fixed deposits or REITs, while your income grows.
- Hold your lifestyle steady as your salary rises, and save the difference.
- Rent while your postings move you around, and buy your first investment property when your income reaches about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month.
- Choose investment units by yield near jobs and transport, not as a future home.
When it does not apply: Property suits people willing to deal with agents, managers, contractors and tenants; if that doesn't suit you, REITs and other assets are reasonable choices. The leverage example assumes the rent covers the instalment, which Sean says to check before buying.

q: How can MK use refinancing, collateral and the rental income to build a lifetime portfolio of ten rental properties?
situation: MK, 23, is a Malaysian with Singapore PR working as a nurse in Singapore, earning about RM100,000 a year. MK's mother recently passed away, leaving three fully paid properties: a two-storey terrace house rented out for RM3,600, a two-storey office lot previously rented for RM5,000, and a single-storey terrace house in Batu Pahat, plus RM150,000 in cash. MK also looks after an elder brother with special needs, whose care costs about RM2,000 a month.
reference:
Sean's words: "Start building from now, assuming you have nothing."
His answer: Not yet. First decide how the brother will be cared for, because that decides where MK works and so what income the banks will see. Then treat the inheritance as untouchable for the next five to eight years, keep the cash safe, and spend that time learning how property investing works before borrowing against anything.
Why:
- Refinancing still needs an income: Paid-off properties can't simply be pushed to a bank for cash: the bank must see enough income to service the new loan. Staying in Singapore or coming home to give care changes that income completely.
- The rent already covers the care: About RM8,600 a month in rent from fully paid properties can pay for professional care, even at RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month, while MK keeps the Singapore career. The mother has already done the heavy lifting.
- A young heir attracts sales pitches: People close to MK know about the inheritance and may push mutual funds, policies or ventures. Whether these are right depends on knowledge MK doesn't have yet, so stay discreet and sign nothing in a hurry.
- The income is already ahead: At 23, MK earns what many in Kuala Lumpur only reach as managers in their late twenties, and Malaysian banks assess Singapore income like a local's. That is a strong base to build on with MK's own credit.
What he told them to do:
- Decide on your brother's care first: yourself, a home helper or a professional facility.
- Keep the RM150,000 in fixed deposit until you know what you want to do with it.
- Work through Sean's four basic steps: set your intent, find your loan eligibility, view properties, then decide.
- Learn how to manage tenants, declare rental income so it counts for future loans, and check that rent covers the instalment.
- When you do borrow, take enough mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) so your loans never pass to your family as debts.
When it does not apply: MK's plans may change within a few years, such as settling in Singapore, where buying an HDB flat would affect how they invest in Malaysia. Sean leaves what and where to buy until MK understands the rules.

q: Is buying a property for its cash back a sensible way to clear the personal loan?
situation: Mr M, 32, and his wife earn about RM15,000 a month after tax between them. In 2022 he took a RM300,000, 10-year personal loan to renovate his parents' house, now RM252,000 outstanding at RM3,300 a month, and they also pay RM2,000 rent. A new launch of about RM1 million offers a RM950,000 loan against a net price of roughly RM730,000, so buying jointly would release about RM220,000 to RM250,000 in cash back. The instalment plus maintenance would be about RM4,700, against the RM5,300 they pay now.
reference:
Sean's words: "In this logic, I would think that it's good."
His answer: Yes, in principle: it swaps a personal loan at about 8% for housing loan debt at 3% to 4%, cuts their monthly outgoings and turns rent into ownership. But first find out exactly when the developer pays the cash back, agree with his wife who carries the new instalment, and ask the bank about settling the personal loan early.
Why:
- The type of loan decides what you pay: Personal loans run at about 6% to 8% and can reach 12%, and credit card balances about 16%, while his newest housing loan is at 3.85%. Sean notes that average property prices have risen about 3.6% a year over 20 years.
- Renovation money doesn't all become value: Putting RM300,000 into a house doesn't add RM300,000 to its price; at most perhaps 30% to 40%, and only for approved extensions that add real space. Borrowing at personal loan rates for that is the costly part of the mistake.
- Timing can make it a triple burden: Rebates are often paid with each stage of construction, but some developers only pay the cash back at handover. If so, the couple would be servicing the new loan's interest, the rent and the personal loan all at once for years.
- It uses up his wife's borrowing power: He only qualifies for about RM750,000 alone, so the plan depends on her name, while she already has a house loan of her own. That limits her future purchases, so the split should be agreed openly.
What he told them to do:
- Ask the developer's senior management, not just the sales staff, exactly when the cash back is paid and put it in writing.
- Ask the bank whether settling the RM252,000 personal loan in one lump sum earns any discount, since its interest may already be fixed.
- Agree with your spouse, in writing if needed, who pays the new instalment when their name is used to qualify.
- Check the rent nearby covers the instalment, as a fallback if you move or need to rent it out.
- Learn how hire purchase, personal and housing loan rates are worked out before taking any new loan.
When it does not apply: Heavy rebates only appear when developers struggle to sell; in a hot market they disappear. If the cash back only comes at handover and you can't carry the overlap, the plan can make things worse rather than better.

q: Is a property a good investment as long as the rent covers the instalment, is he moving too fast on a second unit, and does a completed project with unsold units mean it is a bad property?
situation: Flash is 24 and works in healthcare. He bought a subsale unit in his hometown, fully furnished it and rented it out within four days, with the rent covering the instalment and maintenance. He is now looking at a completed project in i-City, Shah Alam, where the developer still has unsold units with zero down payment and about RM30,000 cash back, and where the rent would also cover the instalment.
reference:
Sean's words: "As long as a rent can cover installment, I'm good."
His answer: At his stage, yes: if the rent covers the instalment and maintenance, the tenant pays off a property he will own outright in about 30 years, even with no price growth. A completed project with unsold units can be the best of both worlds, provided he checks subsale prices and can carry both units empty for six months.
Why:
- The flipping era is over: When Sean started there were developer interest-bearing schemes, no two-loan limit on 90% financing and easy loan approvals, so buyers flipped new launches. Now developers price that gain in, so he plays the equity game: hold units whose rent covers the instalment.
- Strategy depends on your money: Someone with RM5 million in cash compares property with fixed deposits and the S&P 500 and may buy corner-lot landed homes, shop lots or land for capital growth. Rent covering the instalment is the strategy for people who rely on bank financing.
- Completed unsold units remove the guesswork: You can see the orientation, build quality, facilities, existing rents and resident complaints, while still getting developer incentives. Compare with subsale prices for the same size: a cheaper subsale needs about 18% upfront but gives better cash flow.
- Unsold usually means overpriced, not bad: Developers, especially listed ones, often set ambitious prices. Oversupply helps investors because struggling developers offer deals; when everyone is rushing to buy, Sean thinks it is time to stop.
What he told them to do:
- Start in an area you know well, where you understand traffic, schools and local habits.
- Fully furnish a rental unit so it lets quickly.
- Check that a unit has more than one rental option: long-term, room by room, short stay, or per head near students and hospitals.
- Compare the developer's price with recent subsale transactions of the same size before buying.
- Before a second unit, make sure your job is secure and you can carry both units empty for six months.
When it does not apply: This is the cash-flow strategy for buyers relying on loans. Sean expects his own strategy to change as his portfolio grows, towards landed, commercial or industrial property with more risk and more capital.

q: Is that price too high for their income, can he borrow in his name alone, should they buy new now or subsale later, and how can they judge a building's common areas before it is built?
situation: Howard and his fiancée are 26, earn about RM20,000 a month gross between them and have about RM300,000 in liquid assets, with no debts. They live rent-free in a relative's apartment in Seri Kembangan, likely until 2027. They want a new launch of 1,100 sq ft or more at RM700,000 to RM900,000, an instalment of about RM3,500, to raise a family in. His fiancée does not want to rent, or to buy a worn subsale.
reference:
Sean's words: "I think it's a green light to go"
His answer: They can afford it, and his RM10,000 income alone roughly qualifies at three times the instalment. Two conditions: don't pay much above the area's median price, and check that rent for similar units nearby covers about 85% of the instalment, so the home can be rented out when the family outgrows it.
Why:
- The 85% rule protects the upgrade: With an instalment of RM3,500, nearby rents of about RM3,000 show demand for the space. Five to seven years on, with children and perhaps a helper, they will likely want more room and can rent out or sell without a loss.
- Don't overpay for romance: Paying perhaps 10% above the median for a setting they truly value is fine as an informed choice; paying well above it simply because they love a concept is not.
- Banks judge today's income: Banks lend on current income, not future raises. Interest during construction can be avoided with schemes such as HouseKEY, which has fewer developer rebates.
- Learn to read a floor plate: Dimensions are fixed once approved, but finishes are not. Visit completed projects, walk from the car park through the lift lobby and corridor to a unit, and compare dark lobbies and corridors with ones that have voids or daylight.
What he told them to do:
- Compare the project's price per sq ft with the area's median.
- Check rents for similar nearby units against 85% of your instalment.
- Ask developers about completed, unsold units, which offer certainty with some launch perks.
- Visit existing projects, not just sales galleries, and each list three likes and three dislikes.
- Invest some of the RM300,000 rather than leaving it idle.
When it does not apply: In a project that sold well, buying early can pay off: Sean bought his own Bukit Jalil home's first phase at about RM700 per sq ft, and later phases sold above RM1,000. In a slow-selling project, waiting for completion carries less risk.

q: Should he rent a place with a lift, or buy one and give up his goal of owning three properties?
situation: Sam is 27, an engineer earning RM5,000 a month, and lives with his parents in a walk-up public housing flat in Penang. His father's health has worsened and he now needs a wheelchair. Renting a home with a lift would cost RM1,000 to RM1,500 a month; buying would mean about RM400,000 or more on Penang Island, using up his loan eligibility. He had set himself Sean's goal of three properties.
reference:
Sean's words: "I think you should rent first"
His answer: Rent a place with a lift now, since his father cannot wait for a purchase to complete, and rent out the walk-up to offset it. Put property investment aside until he has an emergency fund, insurance and more income; the three properties are meant to come about one a decade, not now.
Why:
- Buying can't solve it quickly: A subsale takes five to six months and about 18% of the price in cash, around RM72,000 on RM400,000, plus RM20,000 to RM30,000 for renovation. A new launch takes three to four years. Renting works almost at once.
- Three properties over 20 years: Sean's goal is one at about 28, one at 38 and one at 48, as income grows. Judging the future by today's salary undersells what a career can earn.
- Investing needs three things first: Six months of expenses saved, covering the parents who depend on him; insurance for himself as the breadwinner; and a clear career path. Property is not a guaranteed win.
- RM5,000 is not a low income: Sean says Sam earns about the average and should stop calling himself low-income. The better question is how to add RM500 or RM1,000 a month.
What he told them to do:
- Rent a unit with a lift for your father now.
- Rent out the walk-up flat to cover part of the new rent.
- Build six months of family expenses in savings and get insurance for yourself.
- Find ways to earn an extra RM500 to RM1,000 a month from your professional skills.
- Revisit buying once you have about RM100,000 set aside and a higher income.
When it does not apply: If he already had about RM100,000 in savings, buying an affordable subsale with a lift could make sense; Sean would not count a family home bought out of need as wasted loan eligibility.

q: Should she buy a new launch or a completed subsale with the money, and how does she make the most of it?
situation: Miss P is 25, earns RM3,500 a month and rents a cheap room in Subang Jaya near work. Her father has offered up to RM300,000 towards a property, as he has done for her siblings, so she has something to fall back on. Her fiancé's family has bought him an apartment in cash, ready well before their wedding in two years. She has been viewing new launches near Subang and PJ, finds the agents pushy, and wonders whether a completed subsale is better.
reference:
Sean's words: "hold on this money for me first until I am ready"
His answer: Not yet. On RM3,500 a month she would be stretched by any loan, so ask her father to hold the money while she researches and raises her income to about RM5,000. Then use it on a subsale or bulk-purchase unit whose rent covers the instalment, and live in the fiancé's apartment.
Why:
- New launches price in the future: Developers know local rents, price a unit you get in three or four years at tomorrow's prices, and since COVID add bigger safety margins. That is why few new launches have rent covering the instalment.
- Subsale needs the cash she has: A RM500,000 subsale needs about RM90,000 up front plus RM35,000 to RM40,000 to furnish, which is what stops most young buyers. Her father's money removes that barrier.
- Keep the gift for investment: Sean would not spend it renovating the marital home, where a simple renovation can cost RM100,000. Her father's purpose is a safe haven for her, so it belongs in a property that pays its own way.
- Twenty viewings make you immune: After visiting about 20 properties across types and areas, you learn what you like and can see sales tactics coming, such as 'only two units left'.
What he told them to do:
- Ask your father whether the money must buy a home, and whether there is a deadline.
- Live in your fiancé's apartment after the wedding and budget for its renovation separately.
- Visit about 20 properties, new and old, high-rise and landed, before deciding.
- Check your loan eligibility, and work to raise your income towards RM5,000.
- Then buy a subsale or bulk-purchase unit whose rent covers the instalment, putting spare cash in the loan account.
When it does not apply: If her father wants the money used now, Sean would still choose a subsale over the new launches she shortlisted. Auctions are best left until after several purchases.

q: Should James refinance the unit to clear the debts, or sell it to clear them and free a 90% loan slot for another purchase?
situation: James is 35 and has held a first property for more than eight years. It is worth about RM430,000, with about RM270,000 left on the loan and an instalment of RM1,330, and rents for RM2,100 a month. James also owns a second property, and over the years has run up about RM70,000 in credit card and personal loan debt, without ever paying late.
reference:
Sean's words: "personally I prefer refinancing"
His answer: Refinancing is better than selling a unit that pays its way every month, but under the newer cash-out rules a conventional refinance may release only about RM30,000, and the existing debts may also hold back approval. So check every route, and settle the high-interest debt quickly even if that means selling.
Why:
- The debts cost four times the mortgage: Credit cards charge about 15% to 18% a year and personal loans roughly 5% to 10%, against about 4% for a housing loan. Swapping one for the other saves a lot, which is why refinancing appeals.
- Refinancing now releases less: Banks lend up to 80% of value, here about RM344,000, which once meant roughly RM74,000 in cash. Now the cash-out portion is assessed over 10 years rather than 35, so only about a third, around RM30,000, may be available; the existing debts also weigh on the debt service ratio.
- Selling gives up a good asset: A quick sale at about RM400,000 would leave about RM130,000 after the loan, enough to clear the debts with RM60,000 to spare. But the unit has risen about 35% in eight years and the tenant pays more than the instalment.
- This is good debt against bad: Housing loans are hard to get because they buy assets; cards and personal loans are easy because banks profit from them, and they are the leading cause of bankruptcy among young Malaysians.
What he told them to do:
- Look up current rates for credit cards, personal loans, fixed deposits and housing loans.
- Ask your bank how much a refinance would actually release under the new cash-out rules.
- Compare a mortgage refinance from an insurer-linked lender, which may assess income more leniently but costs more.
- Settle the card and personal loan debts first, even by selling if no refinance works.
- Find out what caused the debts before buying another property.
When it does not apply: The rules Sean describes are as of late 2024 and he expects them to tighten. Buyers who keep their 90% loan slots full can still buy through bulk purchase, commercial titles or larger down payments.

q: Should he rent the unit out, or put all his debts through AKPK, the debt management agency, to avoid bankruptcy?
situation: Mr Lee has a permanent job, but his credit card, personal loan and housing loan payments now exceed his income. His Rumawip unit in Kuala Lumpur has just been handed over, partly furnished with no furniture, and he cannot afford to fit it out or move in. His CCRIS record is still clean, but he expects to start missing payments within months.
reference:
Sean's words: "the only cure for anxiety is action"
His answer: Rent the unit out and stay where he lived before. Use what credit he has left, or a friendly loan from his parents, to furnish it just enough to let. Go to AKPK only if he cannot keep up, and cut spending and add income straight away, because the cause is overspending, not the property.
Why:
- Owning a home has three costs: The down payment, the monthly instalment and the cost of furnishing. Buyers of new launches often forget the third, and that raises in the years before handover rarely keep up with living costs.
- Rent can carry the unit: Sean expects a Rumawip unit like this to rent for at least its instalment, roughly RM1,800 against RM2,000. A tenant's two-plus-one months' deposit also buys a few months' breathing room.
- Debt for income is different: Borrowing on a zero-interest instalment plan to furnish a unit that then earns rent is not the same as borrowing for gadgets or clothes. If furnishing everything is too much, he can rent out the bigger rooms and live in the smallest.
- AKPK is not bankruptcy: AKPK consolidates card and personal loan debts into one repayment and stops new credit. Missing payments instead leads to warnings, notices and, within about six months to a year, auction; bankruptcy can even cost a job, since you cannot hold a bank account.
What he told them to do:
- Move back to your previous home and put the unit up for rent.
- Furnish only what a tenant needs, using zero-interest instalments, second-hand pieces or a loan from your parents.
- Sell belongings you haven't used in three months, and downsize spending everywhere you can.
- Take on part-time work at weekends and holidays to raise income quickly.
- Before buying a home, set aside the would-be instalment each month to test whether you can carry it.
When it does not apply: Sean is not a licensed financial planner and had no figures for the debts, so the steps are general. Rumawip units carry a five-year moratorium on resale, which is why selling is not an option here.

q: What can they do with a unit that pays nothing and cannot be sold?
situation: Mr K and his sister jointly bought a serviced apartment as an investment, leased back to a hotel operator under a guaranteed rental return. It completed more than four years late; they sued for late delivery and won. The operator, which shared an office with the developer, never paid them; they won judgment against it, but it is a RM2 company. There is still no strata title and no AGM, and unknown companies bill them for utilities and maintenance. They could not find a buyer even at RM210,000 below their purchase price.
reference:
Sean's words: "not all properties make money"
His answer: There is no good way out. They can sell at a deeper loss and pay the bank the difference now, or keep paying the loan and wait on a rescue by a bigger developer that may never come. The real lessons are for buyers who have not yet signed for a scheme like this.
Why:
- Guaranteed returns are priced in: A guaranteed 6% for five years is usually added to the price up front, so a unit worth RM500,000 is sold at about RM650,000 with a large discount. It only works if the operator and developer stay solvent and honest.
- If it's so good, why share it?: A developer with a profitable hotel would run it or partner with another developer. Selling rooms to hundreds of buyers is a way to raise cash from people who want an investment with no effort.
- You may not control your own unit: In a hotel-run building the key cards are held centrally, so owners often cannot rent their unit out themselves.
- Selling below the loan costs cash: If the loan is about RM800,000 and the unit sells for less, the owners must pay the bank the difference in cash. The alternative is to keep paying for years while the unit earns nothing.
What he told them to do:
- Before buying, check that current rents nearby already cover the instalment you will pay at completion.
- Avoid guaranteed-rental-return and hotel-leaseback schemes.
- Avoid buying jointly with a relative unless each of you can carry the loss alone.
- If stuck, work out whether you can afford to sell below the loan before cutting your losses.
- Take complaints about a missing joint management body or strata title to the Commissioner of Buildings, and keep legal advice on disputed bills.
When it does not apply: Sean notes the worst case is the developer winding up altogether; while it is still operating, a takeover by a bigger developer remains a slim chance. For other buyers, distressed sellers in such buildings can be an opportunity if the price falls below replacement cost.

q: Is it a good plan to buy three RM300,000 condos in Kuala Lumpur with RM200,000 down on each, borrowing only RM100,000 apiece, and live on the roughly RM500 a month each would leave?
situation: Mr Lee is 35 and has worked in Singapore for about eight years. Gains from shares during COVID went mostly into a Singapore condo whose rent covers all its costs with a little to spare. He also has several hundred thousand ringgit in cash and savings earning interest, and wants to move back to Malaysia and stop working.
reference:
Sean's words: "Use credit to buy properties, not use capital."
His answer: No. Putting RM600,000 in cash into three condos for about RM1,500 a month is a poor return; the same cash in fixed deposits at about 3% earns that without tenants. Buy with loans while he still has a salary to qualify, keep his capital invested, and don't stop working altogether.
Why:
- The cash would take decades to pay back: RM600,000 for RM1,500 a month takes 400 months to recover. At about 3% a year, the same RM600,000 in fixed deposits pays about RM1,500 a month with no vacancies or bad tenants.
- RM300,000 condos are the wrong stock: At that price in Kuala Lumpur, Sean says, you are mostly looking at welfare-type apartments, which he would leave alone.
- Loans need an income: Malaysia lets buyers borrow up to 90% and still find units whose rent covers the instalment. That needs a salary or declared income to qualify, so buy before quitting rather than after.
- Interest is a cost against rent: Loan interest can be written off against declared rental income, which is one more reason not to pay down so much up front.
What he told them to do:
- Keep the cash in fixed deposits or the investments you already know well.
- Buy one ready-built unit of around RM600,000 whose rent covers the instalment, and try it before buying more.
- Sign for any properties while still employed, then leave the job once the loans are approved.
- Take three to six months off before deciding what to do next, rather than retiring outright.
- Find work you would do even unpaid; Sean argues life is only stressful when you do what you dislike.
When it does not apply: If he has no wish to borrow at all, Sean would still put the cash into safer non-property investments first, because they keep the flexibility a family emergency may need.

q: Will rent paid every six months, rather than monthly, affect his income assessment when he applies for a second property?
situation: Mr J is 26, self-employed in Kota Kinabalu and earns about RM10,000 a month net. His mother spotted a listing in the condo where he lives: RM520,000, partly furnished, with a market value of about RM580,000. The owner wanted a quick sale, so he negotiated it to RM500,000, and the bank valued it at RM650,000. He handled the paperwork himself, did minor renovations and rented it out for about RM200 a month more than his instalment. The tenant now offers to pay RM12,600 every six months for two years.
reference:
Sean's words: "Luck is when opportunity meets preparation."
His answer: Yes, it will. Banks look at rental income month by month in your bank statements, so lump sums or uneven amounts may not be counted, and that can cost him the next property. Ask the tenant to pay the same amount every month instead.
Why:
- Banks want steady monthly credits: When you apply for a loan, the banker reads your statements month by month. Rent that arrives every six months, or varies because repairs were deducted from it, looks inconsistent and may not be recognised as income.
- Keep repairs separate from rent: Letting a tenant fix things and deduct the cost is common, but it breaks the pattern. Sean has repairs fixed and paid separately, while the full rent is still paid to him each month.
- Subsale lets you negotiate: With a subsale or bulk purchase you can counter the asking price; a developer's retail price is fixed. Knowing his own building let Mr J judge a below-market listing and act quickly.
- Stay ready for the deal: Sean checks his own CCRIS and loan eligibility regularly, because good-value listings go to whoever can commit first. A subsale needs about 18% of the price in cash, so savings must be in place before the chance appears.
What he told them to do:
- Decline lump-sum rent if you plan to apply for another loan soon.
- Offer the tenant an auto-debit, or 12 post-dated cheques to bank in each month.
- Pay for repairs separately rather than deducting them from the rent.
- Keep your loan eligibility and CCRIS checked, so you can move when a below-market listing appears.
- Ask for a better price or rate at every step, from the seller to the lawyer and the bank.
When it does not apply: If you don't need the rent counted for a loan in the next year or two, advance payment matters less; the issue is only how a bank reads your statements.

q: Should YK take high cash back with negative cash flow, how is capital growth judged, is buying three units in quick succession overcommitting, and should spare cash go into a flexi loan?
situation: YK is 29, works in a helping profession and earns about RM5,500 a month, with a six-month emergency fund, RM50,000 in savings and comprehensive insurance, and recently joined a bulk-purchase club. YK wants positive cash flow and early retirement, and is weighing a completed unit with high cash back but a monthly shortfall, then two more units soon after.
reference:
Sean's words: "So, my suggestion is to go slow."
His answer: Take positive cash flow over cash back where possible, buy one unit at a time and get each one rented before the next, and build up salary first. Ten properties in ten years on RM5,500 a month is a target nobody else has set.
Why:
- Cash back is borrowed money: It suits someone using it to clear credit card debt at about 18% or a personal loan at about 8%, or a business owner using a flexi loan as cheap working capital. Without that need, a smaller loan with rent above the instalment is better; buyers who spent their cash back are the ones who ended up in auctions.
- Rent sets a high-rise's value: Each RM450 a month of surplus rent supports about RM100,000 more loan over 35 years at 4%. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM950,000, rents for about RM1,500 above its instalment, so the next investor could pay about RM1.25 million and still break even. That surplus mostly happens in tier one locations.
- Studios suit only expensive land: Studios work where land is too costly for bigger units, such as Mont Kiara, Bangsar South and KLCC. In outlying areas they are a mismatch, however cheap they look.
- Active income drives the portfolio: Investors who build portfolios fast usually earn RM30,000 or more. On RM5,500, a RM20,000 repair can hurt. Property keeps you rich; growing income is what makes you rich, and rental income replacing a salary is a goal for 55 or 60, not 35.
What he told them to do:
- Choose a lower loan with positive cash flow over cash back you don't need.
- Rent each unit out before committing to the next.
- Pick one route, subsale, auction or bulk purchase, and execute it rather than joining several courses.
- Put spare cash in a flexi loan unless you can reliably earn more than the loan's 3.8% to 4%.
- Set a goal by monthly cash flow or total value, not a number of units by a deadline.
When it does not apply: For someone with expensive debts to clear, a high cash back unit with a small monthly shortfall can make sense, provided the cash back is kept as a buffer and not spent.

q: Should she invest in property at her age? Should she pay cash or borrow, buy new or subsale, and are these short-stay projects worth it?
situation: Bernadette is over 60. People keep telling her fixed deposits are pointless and EPF returns may disappoint, and she has been shown developer-run short-stay projects in Bukit Bintang and KLCC advertised at 9.2% to 9.6% returns.
reference:
Sean's words: "A bit too late for real estate? Personally, I think so."
His answer: Probably not as a main plan. Property's big advantage is decades of cheap borrowing that tenants help repay, and at 60 that is mostly gone. Low-risk options paying a similar return, without the hassle or locked-up money, suit her better.
Why:
- The leverage advantage is mostly gone: Banks usually cap loans around age 70, so the tenure is short. A RM500,000 loan at 4% costs about RM5,000 a month over 10 years against about RM2,200 over 35. Almost no RM500,000 unit rents for RM5,000.
- Property locks your money up: Selling takes about four to five months for freehold and seven to eight for leasehold, which needs state consent. That is a problem if you suddenly need money for health or an emergency.
- Other assets pay similar returns more easily: RM500,000 in fixed deposits at about 3% pays roughly RM1,250 a month; a property yielding 6% pays about RM2,500 but needs tenants, agents and upkeep. EPF has paid around 6%, and some Malaysian dividend stocks have paid more, with the freedom to sell part at any time.
- Advertised short-stay returns rarely last: High returns usually hold only for the first years. Once a building proves profitable, more owners convert and a price war follows: in one Bukit Bintang project, nightly rates fell from about RM300 to RM120. Only investors buy such units, and authorities can ban short stays, as Singapore and Penang have.
What he told them to do:
- First decide whether this money is spare or what you will live on. If you depend on it, keep it liquid.
- Compare any property yield with fixed deposits, EPF and dividend income before buying.
- If you still earn and do buy for investment, Sean would borrow rather than pay cash, keeping cash for medical costs, with mortgage insurance so no debt passes to your family.
- If you already own a short-stay unit, plan to sell while it is still profitable, typically within five years.
- Be wary of returns quoted by the people selling the unit; get independent advice.
When it does not apply: For someone over 60 with spare capital, experience and other income, property can still work; Sean knows seasoned investors buying offices and land in cash at that age. For younger readers the lesson runs the other way: two or three paid-off properties by 60 can fund a comfortable retirement.

q: From an investment point of view, is selling now the right choice?
situation: Mr G and his then-girlfriend bought a home in Puncak Alam in joint names for own stay, with an SPA price of about RM738,000 after discounts. They have since broken up on bad terms. The unit is now worth about RM650,000 against a loan balance of about RM656,000, so selling means covering a RM6,000 shortfall and about RM10,000 in legal fees. She wants to rent it out unfurnished for about RM1,500 to RM1,700 and sell in five years; he wants to sell now and is considering legal action to exit.
reference:
Sean's words: "Own it. Own the mistake and move on."
His answer: Sell. Holding might work out better on paper, but not for him: two people who can't talk will fight over tenants and costs for years. About RM16,000 is a fair price for a clean slate, even if he pays her share as a farewell gift.
Why:
- Numbers won't settle a feud: Both are accountants, but a spreadsheet won't persuade an ex who wants him out of her life. Each will expect the other to deal with tenants while the rent is split equally, and every conversation will start with blame.
- He made the choices: They paid above nearby prices because it was a dream home, and the slow-growing location was there from the start. Accepting that the property and the partner were his choices is the quickest way out of the trouble.
- Discounts were money from the future: A heavy discount lets you buy without the 18% in cash a subsale needs, but it means paying more than the market's price. Making that back over three to five years, as his friend in an earlier phase has, is a normal result, not a failure.
- Unfurnished units rent cheaply: An empty unit only attracts tenants with very low rent. Owners who plan from the start to spend RM70,000 to RM80,000 furnishing it can rent for more, and the furnishing serves tenant after tenant, but that has to be planned before the keys, not after.
What he told them to do:
- Get quotes from lawyers for the sale costs and budget the shortfall to the bank.
- Sell, even if you end up covering the full RM16,000 yourself.
- Never buy a home in joint names with a boyfriend or girlfriend; if you must buy together, put it in one name.
- If a couple can't afford a home in one name, rent, and each buy a unit of RM400,000 to RM500,000 whose rent covers the instalment.
- If you buy to rent out, plan and save for furnishing before key collection.
When it does not apply: There is no RPGT to pay when selling below the SPA price. And to investors, Sean notes, sellers in this position are where good deals come from, which is why he always knows how much he can borrow.

q: Should he buy the house to run his tuition class downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs?
situation: TG is 35, a government secondary school teacher recently transferred to Kuantan, where he now lives with his wife. He earns about RM6,000 a month, has no debts, RM130,000 in savings and RM30,000 in ETFs and stocks. His wife's own house, due in late 2026, is too small for classes, so he is eyeing the last unsold intermediate double-storey house in a completed Bukit Setongkol project for RM440,000, with the developer paying the SPA legal fees and stamp duty. He would hold it for about 20 years, then retire to Selangor.
reference:
Sean's words: "I want to make money the right way, the legal way."
His answer: Only once he knows he can legally run a tuition centre there. Many do it in houses, but a residential title isn't meant for it, and neighbours, safety and licensing can end the plan. Without the business, the house has to stand as an investment, and its rent won't cover the instalment.
Why:
- A home is not a licensed premises: A proper tuition centre usually rents a shop office, registers a business and meets fire and space requirements. Running one in a house saves on rent, utilities and licences, which is why it is common, but it lasts only until someone is hurt, something goes wrong or a neighbour complains.
- Neighbours bear the cost: Classes of 30 to 100 students bring cars dropping off and picking up every evening, noise at night and heavy use of toilets and water. Some older KL houses on busy roads have been rezoned for business, but they still register as businesses and cost more to maintain.
- Landed rent rarely covers the loan: At RM440,000 the instalment would be about RM2,000 a month, while local rents point to about RM1,500 to RM1,600, so the tenant would pay the interest and he the principal. In small towns people buy as soon as they can afford to, so rents stay low; landed homes earn mainly through price growth of about 3% to 5% a year.
- Rooms for transferred staff can pay: In smaller towns, teachers, doctors and nurses on transfer struggle to find rooms quickly and will pay 20% to 30% more for immediate availability. His network of transferred teachers could fill the house room by room.
What he told them to do:
- Ask the local council whether you can get a licence to run a tuition centre in that house before buying.
- Check rents for double-storey houses in the area; Sean would buy if it could rent for about RM2,000 a month.
- Use your LPPSA housing loan if you go ahead.
- Compare it with a unit of about RM400,000 to RM440,000 in KL whose rent covers the instalment.
- When researching any home, find out what causes the area's traffic jams, such as schools, markets or highway bottlenecks.
When it does not apply: If he simply wants a family home near his wife's relatives to hold for 20 years, buying is reasonable, and the house number 4, which the agent offered to change, doesn't bother Sean. As a teacher on transfer, renting may also be the cheaper choice in a small town.

q: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?
situation: Mr. C is planning his first purchase, a two-bedroom unit in a new Subang Jaya project with strong rent. His plan was to buy where rent covers the instalment and maintenance, then sell after about five years for a gain of perhaps RM100,000. He doubts the long game: older apartments decline, newer projects keep coming, and a RM500 to RM1,000 monthly surplus could turn negative during vacancies or repairs.
reference:
Sean's words: "Don't be too concerned of cash. Build the asset first."
His answer: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.
Why:
- Each RM500 surplus is about RM100,000 of value: A buyer can pay about RM100,000 more and still have rent cover the instalment. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM1 million three years ago with a RM4,000 instalment, should rent for RM5,500 to RM6,000, so he could sell at RM1.2 million to RM1.3 million, but would then have to find somewhere to put the cash.
- Cash loses to inflation: Sean puts real inflation at around 10% to 12%, against about 6% from EPF, so cash shrinks every year. Property hedges inflation: rising building costs, higher wages and lower interest rates all lift the value of what existing owners hold.
- Older units still rent: Older Mont Kiara units first sold at around RM380,000 to RM420,000 still yield about 5% to 5.5% at today's prices, because not everyone can afford new. Whether new beats old still comes down to location and management.
- Tenants and the bank do the work: A break-even portfolio costs Sean about one and a half to two months of instalments a year in agent fees and repairs, roughly five years' worth over a 30-year loan. Five RM300,000 units renting at RM1,500 each would then pay him RM7,500 a month, for working on each unit once or twice a year.
What he told them to do:
- Buy only where rent covers the instalment and maintenance with zero down payment, Sean's strict rule.
- Compare the price with the area's median so you never overpay.
- Look at 20 different properties across the buying channels before settling on this one.
- Use credit for property and put your own capital into other investments.
- Judge any gain as a percentage of what you put in, not as a lump sum.
When it does not apply: The plan fails if the unit bleeds, with rent covering only half the instalment. Nor must you hold to the end: if life changes, such as moving overseas, Sean would sell. And if RM100,000 is large against your savings, taking the gain may be the right call for you.

q: For her third property, should she use cash on a subsale or auction unit with 10% down, or buy new or through bulk purchase, and save her cash?
situation: YX is 30 and single, earns about RM8,000 net from her job and declares about RM5,000 a month from her own marketing business. She shares the loan on a landed own-stay home with her sister and bought a second landed house at auction for RM560,000, financed by an insurer whose loans don't appear in CCRIS, so she still has one 90% loan left. She has RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash and is a member of a property investment club.
reference:
Sean's words: "Use as little of our money as possible."
His answer: Keep the cash and use credit. Sean has no favourite channel; he buys wherever the best deal is, but with her aim of letting the property pay for itself, new launches and bulk purchases fit better than subsale or auction, and her savings are worth more as runway for her business.
Why:
- Less cash in means more options later: A subsale bought with a bigger down payment may give RM500 a month of positive cash flow, while a new unit with a larger loan may only break even. Sean still picks the one that ties up less money, and spends the difference on furnishing the unit so it stands out to the best tenants.
- A bigger discount beats a standard one: Developers give everyone the same standard 10% or so. A bulk purchase with a 20% to 30% discount lets you own the unit, furnish it and still leave your savings untouched; any spare cash can sit in the loan to cut interest while staying available.
- Auctions carry hidden problems: She was lucky with a landed auction house. Of ten auction units Sean has heard about, one or two had problems, and high-rise ones bring questions about arrears, whether the developer still exists and whether the strata title has been issued.
- Her business may out-earn her job: If her side business grows from RM5,000 to RM15,000 a month, it may be time to focus on it. With living costs of about RM4,000, RM400,000 in savings would let her quit and build the business on her terms rather than take every job just to survive.
What he told them to do:
- Make sure the property itself makes sense before choosing how to buy it.
- Compare the same project across all four channels when they overlap, such as just after completion when unsold, subsale and auction units all exist.
- If you have paid for an investment club, use its research and advisers before comparing deals yourself.
- Keep your savings as an emergency fund and business runway rather than spending them on down payments.
- If you are a first-time buyer, stay away from auction high-rises until you understand their risks.
When it does not apply: If you dislike owing the bank a lot, Sean says it is fine to stop at two properties using both 90% loans. And financing from an insurer costs more: the rate is fixed and usually higher, and you must buy insurance from them.

q: Should KB sell some or all of the properties before retiring, move the money into fixed deposits and other assets, and stop dealing with tenants?
situation: KB is 59, a Malaysian who has worked in Singapore for about 35 years and holds Singapore PR. KB owns ten fully paid condos, three in Singapore and seven in Penang, and plans to retire to Penang in two to three years. The Penang units have doubled or tripled in value but yield only 3 to 4%, many are over 20 years old, and good tenants are getting harder to find.
reference:
Sean's words: "So, don't suddenly sell all, pace yourself in selling."
His answer: Selling the Penang units makes sense, perhaps keeping one, but slowly, so the sales aren't taxed as a property business. The three Singapore units are worth keeping for income.
Why:
- Selling fast can be taxed as business: RPGT applies to sales within five years of the SPA date, and the rates change with each Budget. The bigger risk is that many sales in a short time can lead the Inland Revenue Board to treat you as trading, and tax the gains as business income.
- Singapore rent alone can fund retirement: Sean estimates about S$1,000 a month per room, so three units, assuming three bedrooms each, bring in roughly S$8,000 to S$9,000, about RM24,000 to RM25,000, which is more than enough to live very comfortably in Penang.
- Penang's LRT decides what to sell first: Units near an upcoming station may rent and sell better once the line opens, so Sean would hold those until it is completed and sell the others first. Distance from transport isn't always a drawback; some people, Sean included, pay more for quiet.
- Refinancing is no longer the easy exit: Sean's own plan was never to sell but to draw out equity by refinancing every few years. New rules now cap the cash you can take out at RM100,000, or a sum based on a 10-year tenure, which makes selling a more realistic exit.
What he told them to do:
- Sell the Penang units gradually, about one every two years; Sean calls this an unwritten rule among investors, not a law.
- Check the RPGT due on each sale against the current Budget rates before listing it.
- Overlay the planned Penang LRT route on your units, and sell those far from future stations first.
- Refresh the interiors of older units before concluding that tenants won't come.
- Keep the proceeds in low-risk places such as fixed deposits and blue chips, and steer clear of new business ventures and joint ventures with friends or relatives.
When it does not apply: If you want to pass the properties to children, selling isn't the only route: Sean is exploring holding property in a company and passing on shares, though he hasn't settled on how. And for anyone still building a portfolio, his own approach is to refinance and keep, not to sell.
